Q5479.L1t: Inchoate crimes such as solicitation, attempt and conspiracy punish conduct that falls short of a completed target offense.
Q5479.L2t: At common law, conspiracy requires a genuine agreement between at least two persons who each intend to achieve the unlawful objective.
Q5479.L3t: Solicitation is complete the moment a person asks another to commit a crime with intent that it be committed, so later withdrawal does not undo it, but an agent who only feigns agreement and never intends to go through with the plan forms no true agreement.
Q5479.L4t: The wife is guilty of solicitation only, because her request was complete when made but no genuine agreement ever existed to make a conspiracy.
Q5479.L2f: Solicitation at common law is a form of attempt that requires the solicited crime to have actually been begun before liability attaches.
Q5479.L3f: A conspiracy is formed whenever one person proposes a crime and the other verbally assents, even if the assenting person is only pretending and secretly never intends to act.
Q5479.L4f: The wife is guilty of conspiracy to commit murder, because the agent's spoken agreement to the plan was enough to complete the conspiracy.

Q5849.L1t: The hearsay rules govern out-of-court statements offered to prove the truth of what they assert, and they include an exception for business records.
Q5849.L2t: The business records exception requires a foundation, usually from a custodian or other qualified witness, that the records were made at or near the time by someone with knowledge, kept in the regular course of business, and made as a regular practice.
Q5849.L3t: Records are out-of-court statements even when their maker testifies, and computer records need a showing that the process and inputs are reliable, which a bare statement that the records were kept regularly does not supply.
Q5849.L4t: The court will demand a fuller foundation showing the reliability of the computer records before admitting them.
Q5849.L2f: Computer-generated records were barred from evidence in federal courts altogether until a rules amendment in 2000 first allowed them.
Q5849.L3f: A statement falls outside the hearsay rule whenever the person who made it is present and available to testify at trial, regardless of when or where it was made.
Q5849.L4f: The hearsay objection fails because the defendant is the declarant and is available in court.

Q5735.L1t: Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction, and removal allows certain actions filed in state court to be moved to federal court.
Q5735.L2t: Removal is governed by 28 U.S.C. 1441, and a motion to remand based on a procedural defect in removal must be made within thirty days of the notice of removal.
Q5735.L3t: The removal statute gives the power to remove only to defendants, so a plaintiff who chose to sue in state court cannot remove her own case, even when it includes federal claims.
Q5735.L4t: The federal court will send the entire case back to state court because the plaintiff had no right to remove it.
Q5735.L2f: Removal of a federal-question case is allowed only if the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000.
Q5735.L3f: Any party to a state-court action, plaintiff or defendant, may remove it once a federal claim appears in the complaint, provided notice is filed within thirty days.
Q5735.L4f: The court will keep the case, because the removal was timely and the complaint includes federal claims.
